title: Performance Interpretation: The Balcony and the Tomb

findings.claim: A director drawing on physical theatre approaches — as Frantic Assembly did in their 2008 production — might stage the fight as a sequence of highly stylised lifts, falls and slow-motion impacts rather than a realistic sword fight.
findings.context: Lesson attributes a 2008 Frantic Assembly production to Romeo and Juliet.
findings.verdict: WRONG ATTRIBUTION. Frantic Assembly's 2008 production was Othello (premiered Theatre Royal Plymouth, 20 September 2008, co-produced with Theatre Royal Plymouth / Royal & Derngate Northampton, developed at Lyric Hammersmith). Frantic Assembly have no recorded Romeo and Juliet production. The description of stylised lifts, falls and slow-motion staging is accurate for Frantic Assembly's style, but the play is wrong — it is Othello, not Romeo and Juliet.

findings.claim: Mercutio's Queen Mab speech in Act 1 is one of the most demanding extended speeches in the play for a performer.
findings.context: Lesson locates the Queen Mab speech in Act 1.
findings.verdict: CORRECT. Queen Mab speech is in Act 1, Scene 4.

findings.claim: Tybalt's emotional memory directed through precise physical training.
findings.context: Lesson attributes 'emotional memory' as a Stanislavski technique.
findings.verdict: CORRECT. Emotional memory (also called affective memory) is correctly attributed to Stanislavski in the lesson's glossary definition.

title: Plot and Structure: Two-Act Working-Class Tragedy

findings.claim: Blood Brothers is a two-act musical play. Act One covers the twins' childhood (roughly the 1960s); Act Two tracks adolescence into adulthood through the 1970s and early 1980s.
findings.context: Lesson gives approximate decade settings for each act.
findings.verdict: BROADLY CORRECT but slightly imprecise. Wikipedia and LitCharts confirm the twins are born in the late 1950s and die in the early 1980s; Act One ends when the boys are around seven (mid-1960s), Act Two covers teens through adulthood ending in the early 1980s. Calling Act One 'roughly the 1960s' is a simplification — it actually starts before the boys are born (late 1950s), though the childhood scenes are indeed 1960s. The decade framing is an acceptable rough guide.

findings.claim: The Narrator is the play's structural spine. He speaks directly to the audience in what the theatrical practitioner Bertolt Brecht called direct address.
findings.context: Lesson attributes 'direct address' specifically to Brecht as a coined term.
findings.verdict: MINOR IMPRECISION. 'Direct address' is a general theatrical term, not a term specifically coined by Brecht. Brecht's primary associated term is the Verfremdungseffekt (alienation/estrangement effect). Direct address is one of many Brechtian techniques, but saying Brecht 'called' it 'direct address' slightly overstates Brecht's ownership of the term. At GCSE level this is acceptable shorthand.

findings.claim: The prologue presents a tableau of two men lying dead while a grief-stricken woman stands over them.
findings.verdict: BROADLY CORRECT. Multiple sources confirm the opening shows the two dead men and their mother. The lesson's description is a legitimate interpretation — some productions show the bodies on stage, others use stretchers. The grief-stricken woman standing over them is confirmed by multiple summaries (Mrs Johnstone sings 'Tell Me It's Not True'). Not a factual error.

title: Invasion of the Body Snatchers and E.T.: Aliens and Anxiety

findings.claim: Invasion of the Body Snatchers was directed by Don Siegel for Allied Artists in 1956, photographed in monochrome SuperScope by Ellsworth Fredericks, with a score by Carmen Dragon.
findings.context: Lesson credits director, studio, DP, and composer.
findings.verdict: CORRECT. Don Siegel (director), Allied Artists (studio), Ellsworth Fredericks (DP, SuperScope format), Carmen Dragon (composer) — all confirmed by Wikipedia and IMDb.

findings.claim: Don Siegel (later known for Dirty Harry) resisted the studio's decision to add a framing device: a hospital interview in which Miles tells his story to a sceptical psychiatrist.
findings.context: Lesson credits Don Siegel as director of Dirty Harry and describes the framing device.
findings.verdict: CORRECT. Dirty Harry (1971) is confirmed as Siegel's most famous later work. The framing device is confirmed as a hospital scene where Miles speaks to a psychiatrist (Dr. Hill, played by Whit Bissell). Siegel's opposition to the framing device is confirmed by multiple sources.

findings.claim: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial was directed by Steven Spielberg for Amblin Entertainment / Universal in 1982, photographed by Allen Daviau, with a score by John Williams. It was the highest-grossing film at original release of any film to that date.
findings.context: Lesson credits director, studio, DP, composer, and box office record.
findings.verdict: CORRECT. All credits confirmed. E.T. surpassed Star Wars (1977) to become the highest-grossing film of all time, a record it held until Jurassic Park (1993). The 'highest-grossing at original release' phrasing is accurate.

findings.claim: Submarine (2010) is a British coming-of-age film directed by Richard Ayoade, adapting Joe Dunthorne's 2008 novel. Shot in and around Swansea, it was produced by Warp Films and Film4 on a budget of approximately $1.5 million. Cinematographer Erik Wilson and editor Chris Dickens... The film premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival in 2010.
findings.verdict: CORRECT. Director (Ayoade), novel source (Dunthorne 2008), location (Swansea), production companies (Warp Films and Film4), budget (~$1.5m), DP (Erik Wilson), editor (Chris Dickens — though Nick Fenton was co-editor, the lesson is not wrong to name Dickens), Toronto premiere 2010 — all confirmed. One minor note: the film has two editors (Chris Dickens and Nick Fenton) but the lesson names only Dickens, which is an omission rather than an error.

findings.claim: Music: Alex Turner (songs) and Andrew Hewitt (score).
findings.verdict: CORRECT. Alex Turner of the Arctic Monkeys provided the original songs; Andrew Hewitt composed the orchestral score. Both confirmed by Wikipedia and the film's credits.

findings.claim: The lesson repeatedly describes a '1980s-throwback colour palette' suggesting the film merely references the 1980s aesthetically, rather than being literally set in that decade.
findings.context: Lesson's framing of the 1980s palette as stylistic choice rather than period setting.
findings.verdict: MINOR FRAMING ISSUE. The film is literally set in 1980s Swansea (Wikipedia: 'set in 1980s Swansea'), not a contemporary film with a retro aesthetic. The lesson's phrasing — 'a heightened, remembered version of adolescence' and '1980s-throwback colour palette' — implies the 1980s quality is a stylistic choice rather than a literal period setting. This is slightly misleading: the colour palette IS stylised, but the setting is actually the 1980s, not a nostalgic device applied to a contemporary story. Low severity as students could infer the period setting from context.
